LBNL Report#2001653 March 25, 2025 1 Introduction This work was motivated by the observation that activities conducted by the National Nuclear Security Agency (NNSA), as well as numerous other agencies of the United States government (USG), the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), and beyond are interested in technology research and development (R&D) in order to improve capabilities of radiation detection as they relate to their missions’ activities. Such activities that could be relevant for the scene data fusion (SDF) technology [1, 2] include those that involve sensing, locating, identifying and quantifying radioactive and/or nuclear (R/N) material, particularly those that do so in ad hoc configurations. As will be detailed in Sec. 2, the relevance of the SDF technology is due to nature of SDF and its intrinsic feature of quantifying the geometry of an environment while concurrently performing a radiologicalmeasurementandfusingtheenvironmentalandcontextualinformationinatime-frame that is sufficiently prompt that feedback to operators and planning approaches is practical during the measurement; we term this time-frame “near real-time”. LBNL Report #2001653 The SDF measurement paradigm differs significantly from one of the most typical examples of state-of-the-art operation of radiation detectors, which is that of an operator carrying a radiation detector.
